text: System Administration Chapter 5 already covered UI Policies from the admin seat. This lesson goes deeper, into the custom scripts option that the condition builder and UI Policy Actions alone can't express.
As a one-sentence recap: a UI Policy's declarative Actions give you exactly three field effects, evaluated live, with no page reload - visible, mandatory, and read-only.

Every UI Policy also has a Run scripts checkbox. Turn it on, and two new fields appear directly on the policy - Execute if true and Execute if false. These hold real client-side JavaScript functions, onCondition_true and onCondition_false, that fire automatically the instant the policy's condition flips, in addition to any UI Policy Actions already configured.

Both functions receive the same two arguments every time: control, a reference to the policy's own DOM-level context, rarely used directly, and g_form - the exact same client-side form API already familiar from Chapter 2's Client Scripts. Inside either function you can call any g_form method: getValue, setValue, setMandatory, showFieldMsg, addInfoMessage - anything a real onChange Client Script could do.

The real use case is layered logic. The UI Policy condition is already doing the work of deciding when something should happen. Run-scripts lets you attach a small, specific side effect right at that same moment - a warning message, a mandatory flag, a value reset - without building and maintaining a whole separate Client Script just to re-check a condition the policy is already tracking.

One fact carries over unchanged from the admin view: this is still entirely client-side. onCondition_true and onCondition_false run in the browser, against the rendered form. A background script, an Import Set, or a Scripted REST API call never renders that form, so neither the condition nor its scripts ever fire. Scripting a UI Policy makes it smarter about what it does on the form - it does not turn it into server-side enforcement. Next lesson moves to UI Actions - the buttons and context-menu items a developer configures, and the single checkbox that decides whether their script runs on the client or the server.
